The Precious Metal Quandary

Louis-Vincent Gave

Gavekal Research | 10 Aug 2026

The start of the Russia-Ukraine war, or at least the decision by Western countries to seize the reserves of the Russian central bank and freeze the assets of various Russian billionaires, was a dramatic accelerant to the unfolding gold bull market (see What Freezing Russia’s Reserves Means). Suddenly, OECD government bonds stopped being the default “store of value” reserve asset for non-Western countries. As an aggregate, central banks switched from being marginal sellers of gold to being massive buyers. Between 2023 and 2025, central banks as a group purchased more than a thousand tonnes of gold each year. Given that annual global production hovers around 3,500-3,700 tonnes, this price-insensitive, very large, increase in marginal demand had a considerable impact on gold and other precious metals’ prices.So when the Iran-US/Israel war rolled around, the initial gut reaction of many investors was to assume that another war would equate to even more money flowing into gold. Instead, gold prices promptly lost US$1,200 an ounce. The declines in silver and platinum (the prices in both metals have roughly halved since their January 2026 peaks) have been even more brutal:
